description:
Tharsis Labs builds the planning tools humans will need to live and work on Mars.

Our first product, MarsWalk, helps crews explore Jezero Crater safely, turning real NASA data into clear mission decisions before anyone steps outside the habitat.

Founded in Colombia. Built for the Red Planet.
summary:
Marswalk Planner is a web map that plans a safe walk for the first human explorers in Jezero Crater, Mars. It brings NASA orbital imagery (HiRISE, CTX, Viking, MOLA, THEMIS), a 20 m elevation model and Perseverance's real traverse into one layered view, and then turns that data into a plan.

For its first walk, "Follow the leopard spots", the planner picks a flat crew base and computes a walking route to Cheyava Falls, the rock where Perseverance found a potential biosignature in 2024. The route stays under NASA's 20° slope limit for a suited astronaut, and the map reports what a crew needs to decide: distance (1.65 km), walking time (36 min), emergency walkback time (28 min), steepest slope (15.8°), an elevation profile, and the time left for science (4.8 h of a 6 h spacewalk). Five points of interest each have a job: shelter, orientation, safety, science and one out of range. Click any other point and the planner answers GO or NO-GO, with the reason.

Every planning number is cited to a NASA source or clearly marked as our own assumption, so a crew can trust what the map says and know where its limits are.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Marswalk Planner is an interactive map of Jezero Crater that plans a Marswalk (EVA) from start to finish. Open it and you see one complete plan, EVA 01 "Follow the leopard spots": a crew base, a walking route to Cheyava Falls, five points of interest and the numbers a crew needs before stepping outside. Press "Walk the route" and a heads-up display (HUD) preview walks the route for you: distance to go, heading, slope ahead, time back to shelter and radiation dose so far, with warnings before steep ground.

The map also says when not to go. Click any point and the planner computes the walk from the base and answers GO, GO with reduced margin, or NO-GO, with the reason. GO means an emergency walkback of up to 30 minutes; between 30 minutes and 1 hour the margin is reduced; over 1 hour, or on a slope over 20°, it is NO-GO. The 30-minute and 1-hour design cases come from NASA's Apollo-based planning numbers; using them as verdict limits is our own choice. Two fixed examples are on the map: the valley wall (too steep, 20.4°) and the Three Forks sample depot (too far: 5.9 km, a walkback of at least 100 minutes).

Live map: https://mj-rojas.github.io/marswalk-planner/

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain. We take the 20 m/pixel CTX elevation model of Jezero (made for Perseverance's landing) and compute the slope of every cell. The map shows it as a walkability layer: green under 10°, yellow 10–20°, red over 20°.

2. Crew base. A site qualifies only if every slope within 200 m is under 5°. Among those sites, the planner keeps the one with the easiest walk to the science goal.

3. Route. A least-cost path search (Dijkstra) over the slope grid. Steeper ground costs more, and cells over 20° are forbidden, because NASA requires a suited astronaut to handle slopes of up to 20°.

4. Plan. Walking times use Apollo planning speeds: 2.7 km/h for the walk, 3.5 km/h for an emergency walkback, and 1.6 km/h (the real Apollo 15 pace) as the slow case. The EVA is 6 hours long.

THE RESULT

- Route: 1.65 km one way, 97% of it under 10°. Steepest point 15.8°, on the last metres before the rock.

- Time: 36 minutes of walking (62 at the Apollo 15 pace). Emergency walkback in 28 minutes, inside the 30-minute design case.

- Science: 4.8 hours at the rock out of a 6-hour EVA.

- Radiation: about 0.17 mSv for the 6-hour EVA, roughly 8 chest X-rays, using the 0.67 mSv/day measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument in Gale crater. If a solar storm hits, the crew is 28 minutes from shelter.

- Timeline: leave the base at 00:00, reach the rock at 00:36, start back by 05:24 at the latest.

- Why not walk straight: the straight line is shorter (1.42 km) but crosses 350 m of ground over 10° and touches the valley wall at 20.4°. The planned route crosses only 48 m over 10°.

The five points of interest each have a job: the crew base (shelter), the ramp into Neretva Vallis (orientation), the valley wall (safety, a no-go zone), Cheyava Falls (science) and the Three Forks sample depot (out of range, a no-go by distance). Cheyava Falls is where Perseverance found "leopard spots" in 2024, a potential biosignature that is not confirmed. A crew could do what the rover could not: map how far the spots extend, choose the best samples and carry them back.

WHY IT MATTERS

A map for astronauts has to answer practical questions: where is it safe, how long will it take, can we get back in time. We tied every answer to a published NASA number. Where NASA has no number (the 10° "careful" class, the 200 m base radius, the route cost function), the map says it is our own assumption. We think that honesty is what makes a planning tool usable.

KNOWN LIMITS

A 20 m grid smooths out boulders and small scarps, so real local slopes can be steeper. Walking times use flat-ground speeds and do not slow down on slopes. The radiation rate was measured in Gale crater, not in Jezero, and changes with the solar cycle.

TOOLS

- Web map: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet 1.9.4, using a Mars coordinate system and NASA Mars Trek tile services. No server is needed; it runs on GitHub Pages.

- Data processing: Python with NumPy, tifffile and Pillow. Three small scripts build the slope layer, the route and the slope grid used in the browser from the elevation model.

- Open source under the Apache 2.0 license.

NEXT STEPS

Perseverance photos at every stop; mineral maps (CRISM) and weather (MEDA, on Perseverance); an AI-generated briefing for each walk; and the HUD preview (today a simulation on the map) on the helmet visor, with live position.

USE OF AI

The code, the texts and the demo slides were written with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), which also helped find and read the NASA sources. No AI runs inside the map. No image is AI-generated: the photo of the rock is NASA's. The demo video is a screen recording of the live map; its sounds are short tones and a synthetic wind made by the page's own code, not recordings and not AI-generated audio.
